newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN ministers to discuss Burma at May 31 meeting.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN ministers to discuss Burma at May 31 meeting.

text.p: ASEAN foreign ministers, meeting in Kuala Lumpur on May 31, are expected to discuss two key documents covering technical and economic issues on admitting three new members to the group, ASEAN diplomatic sources said on Friday.
The sources expected the ministers to decide when ASEAN would admit Burma, Laos and Cambodia to the now seven-nation organisation, which celebrates its 30th anniversary this year.
"I think basically the decision is going to be made (on May 31)," one source said, adding the three would be admitted in July or December.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has come under strong Western pressure not to admit Burma over what is seen as the lack of democracy and human rights abuses by the military government there.
But the ASEAN nations -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- have rejected U.S.-led efforts to isolate Burma through sanctions.

A senior ASEAN diplomatic source reiterated that Burma's politics were not a question for debate, and noted that ASEAN members decided last year that Burma, Laos and Cambodia would be admitted simultaneously..
"It is not (Burma's) political system that is an issue, it is whether they are ready to fulfill the various treaties and agreements to which ASEAN members adhere," he said.
Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh arrived in Rangoon on Friday for a 24-hour visit aimed at boosting bilateral ties.
Indonesia's President Suharto paid state visits to Laos, Cambodia and Burma in February.

Diplomatic sources said foreign ministers at the May 31 meeting would discuss a report by ASEAN Secretary-General Ajit Singh on technical progress, and a report from senior economic officials following visits to the three prospective members.
The contents of the reports were not immediately known, but some sources said the final decision on admitting them was likely to be a political one.
"ASEAN's policy is that members do not interfere in the internal affairs of other members, and the policy is that we shouldn't be doing it with potential members," one source said.

Diplomatic analysts said Malaysia was keen to admit the three at the annual foreign ministers' meeting being held in Kuala Lumpur in July -- achieving the aim of its founders to include all 10 Southeast Asian nations in the anniversary year.
The other possible date is in December, when ASEAN heads of government meet at an annual informal summit.

Admitting Burma in December could ease tensions over the issue with Western powers -- including the United States -- who attend the ASEAN Regional Forum security enhancement group that meets immediately after the formal foreign ministers' session.
